summary: Mission Possible: Seattle is a cooperative 3D junior astronaut mission trainer for kids ages 9–12. One to four players arrive at a damaged Martian outpost, collect six cassette briefings with NASA photographs, and repair the base as electrical engineers, medics, agriculture specialists, or field engineers. Once the base is running, the crew plans expeditions and keeps power, oxygen, water, food, and radiation exposure in balance. Players see what happens when they spend scarce materials, prioritize one upgrade over another, or wait too long to seek shelter. Archived Perseverance weather measurements and NASA life-support research ground those choices in real mission constraints. The game gives young players a shared goal and a reason to use science, explain their decisions, and revise their plan together.
details:
Mission Possible: Seattle is a first- and third-person cooperative game for one to four junior astronauts. Players arrive outside a damaged outpost and follow gold guides to six cassette briefings. NASA photographs connect the rooms and equipment to real space research. The crew takes on electrical, medical, agriculture, and field engineering roles and restores the base through hands-on tasks.

After the repairs, players manage daily operations and plan field trips. The crew shares power, water, oxygen and food, weighs upgrade choices against limited materials, and uses a rover or drone to scout. Dust can reduce solar generation. Solar storms make shelter and radiation exposure part of expedition planning. When a vital system fails, the game explains what ran out so the crew can try a different strategy.

The game helps kids ages 9–12 practice systems thinking. A decision about solar power can change whether the greenhouse and life support keep running. Each player can bring a different piece of information to the team and explain what they think the crew should do. We hope it can support a classroom or family discussion about how astronauts plan a mission.

We built the low-poly 3D world in Godot 4.7.2 with GDScript and used Blender for modeling and asset editing. We used ENet for LAN multiplayer, TwoVoIP for voice, Python and PowerShell for build and test tools, and Git LFS for large assets. Room-based activation, view culling and distance-based detail help the game run smoothly.

AI disclosure: We used Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to assist with GDScript, build and test scripts, design documentation, and research summaries. Our team directed the game design and integration. The repository documents scientific sources and asset credits.
